case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of left-sided jaw swelling with insidious onset. It was not associated with pain, fever, or functional debilitation. The patient’s parent reported that the swelling had resolved with an unidentified oral over-the-counter medication and then recurred 5 times during the 2 years. The patient was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a palpable hard mass, approximately 5 × 4 cm in size, at the left ramus of the mandible. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the patient’s neck revealed an expansile lesion involving the left ramus of the mandible with ground glass matrix, thickened overlying cortex, and lamellated periosteal reaction (Figure 1). The left masseter was diffusely swollen with ill-defined hypodensities within it. A technetium-99m bone scan showed uptake within the mandibular lesion. Fine-needle aspiration cytology results showed the presence of macrophages, lymphocytes, and a few polymorphs, but no atypical cells. Given that the mass was clinically suggestive of a malignant neoplasm, an ultrasonography-guided biopsy procedure of the mass was performed. Histopathologic examination of the specimen showed chronic inflammatory infiltrate without any evidence of a malignant tumor.
case_info.caption: Coronal reconstruction of computed tomography (CT) image of bone window showing expansion of the left mandibular ramus (A). Axial bone window image (B) showing underlying bone sclerosis (arrowhead) and overlying lamellated periosteal reaction (asterisk).
case_info.explanation: After radiopathologic correlation, the final diagnosis was chronic Garré sclerosing osteomyelitis (GSO).1This is a rare and specific form of chronic osteomyelitis with proliferative periostitis, characterized by periosteal reaction in the form of cortical thickening and a related loss of the bony medullary canal (Figure 2). When first described in 1893,1it presented some initial confusion regarding the existence of suppuration or sequestration. GSO commonly affects males in childhood or early adulthood,2with the mandible being most commonly involved.3 Poor oral hygiene and secondary periodontal issues, such as odontogenic infections or moderate periodontitis, may be associated with the cause of GSO. Dental extraction has been described as a potential risk factor.4Symptoms are gradual and appear over several months as recurrent, nonprogressive, and episodic pains without any substantial functional loss of the involved bone.5The disease usually presents with no active signs of infection.2Larger lesions may develop swelling and asymmetry.3Notably, the duration of GSO is variable among patients and may even occur over several years. Most patients are relatively healthy between clinical episodes.6Although the disease has a low risk of mortality, it has been associated with a high degree of morbidity in some cases. The causes of GSO are unclear but they are thought to involve a low-virulence bacterial species. Even after treatment, infection can persist and perpetuate the chronic process. There are no specific diagnostic criteria for GSO, and diagnosis is usually based on imaging findings in combination with a clinical history of a prolonged disease course. Laboratory test results may occasionally show elevated inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Radiography findings demonstrate cortical thickening with medullary sclerosis.3Computed tomography imaging may be more sensitive in demonstrating the bony expansion and may also reveal redundant periosteal layering of the cortex (onionskin appearance).6The imaging features in GSM are attributed to repeated irritation and inflammation of the periosteum, secondary to the low-grade chronic infection. Results of isotope scans may also show increased uptake at the site of involvement.2Although imaging results indicative of Ewing sarcoma may be similar, distinguishing characteristics of GSO are the acuity of the swelling along with local site discomfort and tenderness.7Cortical thickening and periosteal reaction may be seen in a primary bone lymphoma (PBL); however, PBL is uncommon in children younger than 10 years and it is usually accompanied by localized pain and B symptoms (ie, associated with lymphoma).8Bony expansion and sclerosis may be seen in fibrous dysplasia; however, there will be absence of overlying periosteal reaction, unless there is a pathologic fracture.9 Histopathologic findings for GSO are inconclusive and may show chronic nonspecific inflammation.10Although low-virulence bacteria are the culprits in most cases, results of cultures are usually negative.5Polymerase chain reaction testing can be requested for diagnosing the causative organism when clinical suspicion is high.6Occurrence of a lesion of this nature in a pediatric patient demands an aggressive workup—without proper clinical context, imaging may mimic a more sinister lesion such as Ewing sarcoma. Other pathologies with a similar presentation include osteoid osteoma, eosinophilic granuloma, and osteosarcoma.2Ultimately, in this patient we diagnosed GSO based on the findings of the physical examination, normal laboratory test results, nonspecific histologic results, and typical radiographic abnormalities in this patient. Treatment of GSO usually involves symptomatic management and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics.2Surgical interventions are only considered for individuals who do not respond to standard treatments because the necrotic-sclerotic bone and its associated blood supply may prevent antibiotics from reaching the infected tissues.3,6Furthermore, the use of endodontic therapy may be an alternative or substitute treatment4given that it does hold promise; however, further studies are needed to compare it with other treatment modalities.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[Case]
A 9-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of left-sided jaw swelling with insidious onset. It was not associated with pain, fever, or functional debilitation. The patient’s parent reported that the swelling had resolved with an unidentified oral over-the-counter medication and then recurred 5 times during the 2 years. The patient was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a palpable hard mass, approximately 5 × 4 cm in size, at the left ramus of the mandible. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the patient’s neck revealed an expansile lesion involving the left ramus of the mandible with ground glass matrix, thickened overlying cortex, and lamellated periosteal reaction (Figure 1). The left masseter was diffusely swollen with ill-defined hypodensities within it. A technetium-99m bone scan showed uptake within the mandibular lesion. Fine-needle aspiration cytology results showed the presence of macrophages, lymphocytes, and a few polymorphs, but no atypical cells. Given that the mass was clinically suggestive of a malignant neoplasm, an ultrasonography-guided biopsy procedure of the mass was performed. Histopathologic examination of the specimen showed chronic inflammatory infiltrate without any evidence of a malignant tumor.

case_info.explanation: After radiopathologic correlation, the final diagnosis was chronic Garré sclerosing osteomyelitis (GSO).1This is a rare and specific form of chronic osteomyelitis with proliferative periostitis, characterized by periosteal reaction in the form of cortical thickening and a related loss of the bony medullary canal (Figure 2). When first described in 1893,1it presented some initial confusion regarding the existence of suppuration or sequestration. GSO commonly affects males in childhood or early adulthood,2with the mandible being most commonly involved.3 Poor oral hygiene and secondary periodontal issues, such as odontogenic infections or moderate periodontitis, may be associated with the cause of GSO. Dental extraction has been described as a potential risk factor.4Symptoms are gradual and appear over several months as recurrent, nonprogressive, and episodic pains without any substantial functional loss of the involved bone.5The disease usually presents with no active signs of infection.2Larger lesions may develop swelling and asymmetry.3Notably, the duration of GSO is variable among patients and may even occur over several years. Most patients are relatively healthy between clinical episodes.6Although the disease has a low risk of mortality, it has been associated with a high degree of morbidity in some cases. The causes of GSO are unclear but they are thought to involve a low-virulence bacterial species. Even after treatment, infection can persist and perpetuate the chronic process. There are no specific diagnostic criteria for GSO, and diagnosis is usually based on imaging findings in combination with a clinical history of a prolonged disease course. Laboratory test results may occasionally show elevated inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Radiography findings demonstrate cortical thickening with medullary sclerosis.3Computed tomography imaging may be more sensitive in demonstrating the bony expansion and may also reveal redundant periosteal layering of the cortex (onionskin appearance).6The imaging features in GSM are attributed to repeated irritation and inflammation of the periosteum, secondary to the low-grade chronic infection. Results of isotope scans may also show increased uptake at the site of involvement.2Although imaging results indicative of Ewing sarcoma may be similar, distinguishing characteristics of GSO are the acuity of the swelling along with local site discomfort and tenderness.7Cortical thickening and periosteal reaction may be seen in a primary bone lymphoma (PBL); however, PBL is uncommon in children younger than 10 years and it is usually accompanied by localized pain and B symptoms (ie, associated with lymphoma).8Bony expansion and sclerosis may be seen in fibrous dysplasia; however, there will be absence of overlying periosteal reaction, unless there is a pathologic fracture.9 Histopathologic findings for GSO are inconclusive and may show chronic nonspecific inflammation.10Although low-virulence bacteria are the culprits in most cases, results of cultures are usually negative.5Polymerase chain reaction testing can be requested for diagnosing the causative organism when clinical suspicion is high.6Occurrence of a lesion of this nature in a pediatric patient demands an aggressive workup—without proper clinical context, imaging may mimic a more sinister lesion such as Ewing sarcoma. Other pathologies with a similar presentation include osteoid osteoma, eosinophilic granuloma, and osteosarcoma.2Ultimately, in this patient we diagnosed GSO based on the findings of the physical examination, normal laboratory test results, nonspecific histologic results, and typical radiographic abnormalities in this patient. Treatment of GSO usually involves symptomatic management and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics.2Surgical interventions are only considered for individuals who do not respond to standard treatments because the necrotic-sclerotic bone and its associated blood supply may prevent antibiotics from reaching the infected tissues.3,6Furthermore, the use of endodontic therapy may be an alternative or substitute treatment4given that it does hold promise; however, further studies are needed to compare it with other treatment modalities.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.

    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.
